source.title: Interpreting the Second-Order Effects of Neurons in CLIP
source.authors: Yossi Gandelsman; Alexei A. Efros; Jacob Steinhardt

page_placements.theme: Self-repair invoked to explain small ablation effects in CLIP vision transformers

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports a mean-ablation comparison bearing on self-repair, but studies indirect effects of neurons in CLIP's image encoder rather than the language-model attention components and measures named in the claim.
record.gate_note: Table 1 compares mean-ablation outcomes for indirect and second-order neuron effects; the text explicitly attributes the smaller performance drop for indirect effects to self-repair. The variance-explained comparison is not a direct measure of the claimed compensation and is not included as a row. Other ablations, adversarial examples, and segmentation results do not test these claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study is about interpreting CLIP ViT image-encoder neurons with a 'second-order lens'. Self-repair, citing McGrath et al., is used only as motivation: Table 1 shows mean-ablating layer-9 indirect effects drops accuracy less than ablating second-order effects. The authors attribute this gap to self-repair but never measure compensation. The two ablations are different quantities: second-order ablation edits the output representation directly, bypassing any downstream computation. Neither ablation has an unablated reference in the table. All versions concern language-model components (attention layers, heads, late MLPs, LM mechanisms) or LM ablation practice. This is a vision encoder's MLP neurons, and the comparison mainly shows their own method's advantage.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with one qualification. The authors conclude that the second-order lens reveals neuron function that indirect-effect ablation hides. They attribute the smaller accuracy drop under indirect-effect mean-ablation (52.3 vs 29.6) to self-repair, but they assert this rather than measure it. The paper's main conclusions concern sparse, polysemantic neuron decompositions, adversarial image generation and zero-shot segmentation.
record.recipe_differences: Uses mean ablation of indirect neuron effects in CLIP's image encoder and compares it with mean ablation of defined second-order neuron effects; it does not reproduce the language-model attention-component interventions in the original sources.

fits_no_version.finding: In CLIP ViT-B-32 layer 9, mean-ablating all neurons' indirect effects leaves 52.3% ImageNet accuracy versus 29.6% when ablating their second-order effects. The authors attribute the smaller drop to self-repair.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Self-repair-like compensation obscures neuron ablation effects in vision transformers (CLIP image encoder).

record.problems: The claim-relevant comparison is for one model and one layer. Table 1 does not report an unablated accuracy or uncertainty for these results, and it does not compare mean ablation with zero or resample ablation.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results left out. Table 1's variance-explained values are not a direct measure of compensation; the paper's other ablation figures concern second-order effects or attention effects rather than self-repair.

untested.parts: No attention-layer ablation or downstream-layer compensation measured in a language model.
No late-MLP erasure of the top token.
No single-head ablation on text, across families or sizes.
No per-input variation or overcorrection measured.
Mean ablation only, no contrast with zero ablation, and not on LM components.
No LM attribution scores compared with true component effects; the CLIP comparison is the authors' interpretive motivation.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'tests'/T2 and its V6/V7 support labels are overreach. The study never compares ablation types, and the self-repair explanation is a single sentence of interpretation. The table also lacks an unablated reference; Figure 3's baseline sits around 60%.

versions.untested_parts: No attention-layer ablation or later-attention-layer compensation is tested.
No late-MLP downregulation of a maximum-likelihood token, or change in erasure after earlier-component ablation, is tested.
No single-attention-head ablation or full-distribution compensation across text prompts, model families, or sizes is tested.
Prompt-level variation and overcorrection in compensation are not measured.
The listed mechanisms—backup heads, copy-suppression heads, final LayerNorm rescaling, and anti-erasure neurons—are not tested as self-repair mechanisms.
The paper reports mean ablation, but does not compare mean or resample ablation with zero ablation; resample ablation and the claim's language-model components are not tested.
The comparison concerns neuron effects in one CLIP image-encoder model and ImageNet validation accuracy, not language-model components or other attribution measures.

rows.subject: OpenAI ViT-B-32 CLIP
rows.operation_detail: Mean-ablate the indirect effects of layer 9 neurons; the paper describes indirect-effect intervention as replacing neuron activations with precomputed per-token means.
rows.measure: ImageNet zero-shot classification accuracy after mean ablation
rows.locator: Table 1; Section 3.3, Comparison to indirect effect
rows.note: The authors state that mean-ablating indirect effects causes a smaller performance drop due to self-repair. The table does not give the unablated accuracy; the reference is the second-order ablation result.
rows.check: The CLIP ViT-B-32 vision encoder's MLP neurons are not the language-model components any version names. The 'baseline' (29.6) is the second-order ablation, a different intervention, not a no-ablation or no-compensation control. Compensation cannot be read from this comparison; the self-repair reading is the authors' assertion.

relation.reason: Self-repair supplies the rationale for avoiding indirect-effect analysis. The authors attribute the accuracy gap to it without independently testing the repair mechanism.

tranche.reason: The study motivates its second-order lens using self-repair and reports method comparisons and applications; it does not isolate or quantify compensation.

source_check.notes: Table 1 reports 52.3% and 29.6% after different ablations, without an unablated accuracy in that table. The appendix's AI-directed text is an example experimental prompt, excluded from the instruction flag.
